title: The Heckscher Museum of Art
summary: Home to Jeremy Dennis’s Weeckatuck from On This Site. Explore Native landscape photography, Shinnecock art, and Eclipse of the Sun Now, September 26, 2026–May 9, 2027.

why_this_matters: The woodland path in Weeckatuck holds a history that a scenic view alone cannot tell. Jeremy Dennis’s photograph brings the memory of a Shinnecock community into the museum, while Courtney M. Leonard’s porcelain map connects Long Island’s shape with the touch of a maker’s hand. These works invite visitors to see a landscape through the people, names, and relationships it carries.
introduction_title: On This Site in the permanent collection
introduction_content:
A woodland path becomes a way into the Native history of Long Island’s South Fork. Part of Dennis’s On This Site project, Weeckatuck recalls a Shinnecock community around present-day Trout Pond in Noyack. In the museum’s audio guide, Dennis describes returning to ancestral places through photography as an act of memory and continued presence.[1]

Read the Weeckatuck place history or hear Dennis discuss the photograph in the museum’s guide.

Eclipse of the Sun Now

September 26, 2026–May 9, 2027

Weeckatuck is included in this exhibition marking the centenary of George Grosz’s 1926 painting Eclipse of the Sun. The show brings politically engaged works from the Heckscher and Art Bridges collections together around war, civil rights, immigration, media, and the environment. Dennis’s photograph brings the remembrance of Indigenous places into that conversation.[1][2]

The photograph belongs to the museum’s permanent collection; this exhibition has a limited run. Check the exhibition page when planning a visit.
history_title: Native artists and changing views of the land
history_content:
Matinecock land and continuing presence

The museum stands within Matinecock traditional territory. Its land acknowledgement recognizes the Matinecock Tribal Nation’s continuing presence, the harms of dispossession, and the museum’s responsibility to become more inclusive. This relationship connects the Huntington museum to the living Native communities whose artists and knowledge shape its programs.[3]

Richard Mayhew: landscape as feeling

Richard Mayhew: Reinventing Landscape, January 20–April 24, 2022, surveyed six decades of painting by the Amityville-born artist of African American and Native American heritage. His luminous landscapes use color and atmosphere to evoke experience rather than simply describe a view. The museum’s collection includes Pescadero (2014), purchased with support from the Town of Huntington Art Acquisition Fund.[4]

An April 5, 2022 virtual Environmental Justice panel paired historian Mark Chambers with Shinnecock artist Jeremy Dennis to connect the exhibition with questions of land, race, and environmental responsibility.[4]

Viewfinders and Indigenous landscape photography

The 2023 exhibition Viewfinders: Photographers Frame Nature included Dennis’s work. Its brochure discusses how On This Site restores Indigenous histories to landscape photography, a field whose earlier surveys often left Native people out of the picture. Photographs become an invitation to learn who has lived in a place and whose account shapes what we see.[5]

Courtney M. Leonard: water, clay, and Shinnecock knowledge

Courtney M. Leonard: LOGBOOK 2004–2023, June 10–November 12, 2023, was the Shinnecock artist’s first retrospective. Ceramic works, paintings, video, and installations brought together Indigenous knowledge, colonial history, and ecological change.[6]

For the exhibition, the museum commissioned CONTACT 2,023…, a large map of Long Island made with thousands of porcelain thumbprints. Its shell-like forms, colors, and patterns draw connections between wampum and European ceramics. The work entered the museum’s collection. A companion Leonard installation at Planting Fields was presented at that separate venue.[6]

Shinnecock art and environmental activism

On October 21, 2023, Leonard joined Shinnecock birthworker and community organizer Ahna Red Fox for Shinnecock Art & Activism. Their conversation, moderated by curator Karli Wurzelbacher, explored motherhood and environmental action. Red Fox’s work with the Neetuonk Garden Project connected the discussion to food sovereignty and community care.[7]
whereintheworld_content:
Find the museum at 2 Prime Avenue, Huntington, NY 11743, in Heckscher Park. Use the museum’s visiting information for current hours, admission, accessibility, and directions.[8]

Continue with Jeremy Dennis, Weeckatuck, and Ma’s House to follow the relationships between contemporary art, community, and place.
